en: The Sūtra on the Intermediate State (Antarābhava-sūtra), Scroll One, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Later Qin Dynasty.

Chapter One: The Tathāgata’s Five Great Vows for Entering the Intermediate State to Teach and Transform Beings. Chapter One: The Tathāgata’s Five Great Vows for Entering the Intermediate State to Teach and Transform Beings.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at the site of the cremation forty-nine paces north of the twin trees in Kapilavastu.
At midnight on the eighth day, when the morning star appeared, the Tathāgata suddenly relinquished his fragmented bodily relics (śarīra) in accordance with the five great vows of all Buddhas:
At the moment of his birth, heaven and earth shook in six ways, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all came to provide assistance; this is called the first dharma of the great vow.
What are the six ways in which they shook?

The east surged and the west subsided; the west surged and the east subsided; the north surged and the south subsided; the south surged and the north subsided; when all four sides surged, the center subsided; and when the center surged, the four sides subsided.

When the Tathāgata first lifted one foot and took seven steps, the entire world shook greatly, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all came to provide assistance; this is called the second dharma of the great vows.
The Tathāgata proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree and sat cross-legged, vowing:
"I shall not rise from this seat until I have attained Buddhahood.
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all came to provide assistance; this is called the Dharma of the Three Great Vows.

Although Pāpīyan heard the name of the Tathāgata, his mind was not cowed; by the power of his vow, heaven and earth shook greatly, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all came to assist him—this is called the Dharma of the Four Great Vows.

The Tathāgata relinquishes his physical body and lifespan, manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa and proceeding into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to teach and transform sentient beings. At that time, heaven and earth tremble greatly, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all come to exhort and praise him; this is called the Dharma of the Five Great Vows.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Fire-Flame Samādhi, leaving behind his fragmented bodily relics, and sat upon a precious lotus flower seven fathoms above the ground. He caused immeasurable, limitless *nayuta* of sentient beings—gods, nāgas, spirits, asuras, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, humans, and non-humans—all to behold the Tathāgata seated upon the precious lotus flower.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra in verse, saying:
"Throughout incalculable kalpas, I have nurtured you, the element of earth.
Now I depart from you; It is as joyful as a snake shedding its skin."
Within the cycle of birth and death across the five realms, there is nowhere you are not present;
though for a time you may appear separated, you are in truth quiescent and without attachment.
Your majestic spiritual power reaches down to the very earth; were it not for you, none could attain liberation.

"Alas! The suffering of separation; bound by the continuous chain of birth and death, may the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas receive them, so that those delivered shall be incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).

At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One emitted eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of light rays from the crown of his feet up to the *uṣṇīṣa*. They universally illuminated the trichiliocosm, reaching upward to the limits of space. All sentient beings therein beheld the radiance; some followed the light and came, while others were sent by various Buddhas to arrive in this Sahā world.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected within himself:

"This intermediate state form is extremely subtle; only a Buddha, a World-Honored One, alone can perceive it. However, these sentient beings—whether they be those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or those abiding in the first stage, the second stage, up to the ninth stage—are not able to perceive it through their own range."

I shall now, by means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, enter the Samādhi of Illuminating Radiance, so that the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—may behold this subtle form.

At that time, the World-Honored One next entered the Samādhi of Non-obstruction and observed the sentient beings within this realm of space—those who are born and those who perish—according to the prohibitions and precepts practiced by all Tathāgatas: as empty, non-existent, and tranquil. He contemplated the perception of impurity, the one hundred and seventy modes of practice, the causal conditions for the root of suffering, and even the twelvefold fetters of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Now I shall enter the subtle, The extremely fine form of the intermediate state (antarābhava),
To transform those classes of sentient beings, Twofold more than those in Jambudvīpa."
The mark of permanence is without attachment; the mark of bliss is empty and without fixedness.
Establishing the roots of the Way and its virtue, one casts off life without defilement.
Having followed this path for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*), one delivers those beings who are difficult to save.
How much more so for this subtle and wondrous form?
There is nothing more difficult than this.
My heart of great resolve is now free from confusion and untainted by any defilement.
"The root of the bodhi-virtues, the ultimate dharma of the brahma-conduct.

Then, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One again emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which universally illuminated immeasurable and limitless *nayuta* worlds in the eastern direction;
and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his radiance, which circled the Buddha seven times before entering through the crown of his head.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How wonderful, World-Honored One!"
Never before heard of, never before seen:
what are the physical forms of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) like? What are their lifespans, their food and drink, and their beauty or ugliness?
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The World-Honored One said, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain each point to you in detail."
"Maitreya, how much milk does a child born in Jambudvīpa drink from its mother’s breast while being held in her arms from birth until the age of three?
Maitreya replied:
“Excluding the portion of blood consumed within the mother’s womb, they drink one hundred and eighty *hu* of milk.
A child born in Pūrvavideha drinks one thousand eight hundred *hu* of milk from the moment it falls to the ground until it reaches three years of age;
a child born in Aparagoyānī drinks eight hundred and eighty *hu* of milk [during that same period].”

In Uttarakuru in the north, when a child is born, he falls to the ground and sits at the crossroads; passersby offer their fingers for him to suck, and in seven days he becomes an adult, for that land has no milk;
beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) subsist by inhaling wind.

"The lifespan of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa is one hundred years; in Pūrvavideha it is five hundred years; in Aparagoyānī it is two hundred and fifty years; in Uttarakuru it is one thousand years; and the lifespan of beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) is seven days."

"The faces of the people of Jambudvīpa are broad above and narrow below; those of the people of Pūrvavideha are perfectly round; those of the people of Aparagoyānī are narrow above and broad below; those of the people of Uttarakuru are square; and the faces of beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) resemble those of the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven."
From this point onward, the name Śākyamuni has ceased, and the Tathāgata of Sublime Enlightenment appears in the world.

This Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, sits upon a precious lotus flower in mid-air and emits the radiance of his tongue-mark, illuminating eighty-seven billion Ganges-sands of worlds in the eastern direction.
That land is named Transformation; its Buddha is named Solidity, who is fully endowed with the ten titles and teaches by means of the One Vehicle.
Seeing this radiance, he addressed the bodhisattvas and the sons of noble families: "Do you all see this radiance?"
He replied, “Indeed, I have seen it,
World-Honored One!”
"I do not understand from where this light comes; which Buddha’s radiance is it that illuminates this world?

That Buddha replied, "To the west, at a distance of eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands of worlds away, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is titled Śākyamuni. He has now attained parinirvāṇa and, having relinquished his physical remains as *śarīra*, desires to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to teach and transform beings. This is the radiance of that Wondrously Enlightened Tathāgata."
"If you wish to go, now is precisely the right time.
At that time, one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas from that land, having received the Buddha’s instructions, arrived in this Sahā world.
The Buddha told him:
"When you reach that land, pay homage, serve, and make offerings; do not harbor indolence or pride. Bear my name and inquire after the Well-Awakened Tathāgata, asking:
'Are you dwelling in ease and vigor? Is your movement firm and strong?'"
The Bodhisattva received these instructions, prostrated at the feet of that Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and suddenly vanished, arriving in this Sahā world.
Eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands of worlds to the south of here is a world named Liberation; its Buddha is named True Purity Tathāgata, who is endowed with the ten titles.
He addressed the bodhisattvas: "Do you see this radiance?"
He replied, "Indeed, I have seen it; I do not know whose Buddha-light this is that illuminates this world.
That Buddha said to him:

"To the north, eighty-seven billion *Ganges* river-sands of worlds away, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni; he has now attained parinirvāṇa and, having relinquished his physical relics, desires to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to teach and transform beings. This is the radiance of that Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment."
"If you wish to go, now is precisely the time.
At that moment, one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas from that land, having received the Buddha's instruction, arrived in this Sahā world.
The Buddha told him:
"When you arrive in that land, attend upon and make offerings to him in person; do not harbor any negligence or pride. Bear my name and inquire after the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment, asking:
'Are you dwelling in ease and comfort? Is your movement vigorous?'"
The Bodhisattva accepted the instruction, prostrated at the feet of that Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and suddenly vanished, arriving in this Sahā world.

Eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands of worlds away to the north, there is a world named Vaidūrya where the Buddha is named Ghoṣadatta Tathāgata, endowed with the ten titles, who addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Do you all see this radiance?"
He replied, “Indeed, I have seen it; however, I do not know whose Buddha-light this is that illuminates this world.
That Buddha said to him:

"To the south of here, past worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty-seven billion Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni; he has now attained parinirvāṇa and, having relinquished his physical relics, desires to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to teach and transform beings. This is the light of that Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment."
"If you wish to go, now is precisely the right time.
At that moment, one billion three hundred million bodhisattvas from that land, having received the Buddha’s instruction, arrived in this Sahā world.
The Buddha told him:
"When you arrive in that land, pay homage, serve, and make offerings there; do not harbor any indolence or pride. Bear my name and inquire after the Well-Awakened Tathāgata, asking:
'Are you dwelling in ease and comfort? Is your movement vigorous?'"
The Bodhisattva accepted these instructions, prostrated at the feet of that Buddha, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and suddenly vanished, arriving in this Sahā world.

Eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands of worlds away to the northeast lies a world named Void Purity (*Kha-viśuddha*); the Buddha there is named Space Treasury (*Gaganagañja*), who is endowed with the ten titles, and there are one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas.

Eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands of worlds away to the southeast lies a world named Blazing (*Jvalita*); the Buddha there is named Vast Manifestation Tathāgata (*Vistīrṇapratibhāsa*), who is endowed with the ten titles, and there are one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas.

To the southwest, at a distance of eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands from here, there is a world named Star-Constellation (*Tārakā*). The Buddha there is named Moonlight (*Candraprabha*) Tathāgata, complete with the ten titles, and he has one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas.

To the northwest, at a distance of eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands from here, there is a world named Destroying Māra (*Mārabhañjana*). The Buddha there is named Valiant Subduer (*Vīravijaya*) Tathāgata, complete with the ten titles, and he has one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas.

Above, at a distance of eighty-seven billion *Ganges* sands from here, there is a world named Ocean Trace (*Sāgarapada*). The Buddha there is named Supreme Excellence (*Paramasūkṣma*) Tathāgata, complete with the ten titles, and he has one hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas.

Eighty-seven billion *Ganges* river-sands of worlds below this place, there is a world named *Prativedha*. Therein dwells a Buddha named Abhayasvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He addressed the bodhisattvas: "Do you see this radiance?"
He replied, "Indeed, I have seen it; however, I do not know whose Buddha-light this is that illuminates this world.
That Buddha said to him:

“In the upward direction, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty-seven billion Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni. He has now attained parinirvāṇa and, having relinquished his physical remains and relics, desires to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to teach and transform beings; this is the radiance of that Tathāgata of Sublime Enlightenment.”
"You all wish to go; now is precisely the right time.
One hundred and thirty billion bodhisattvas from that buddha-field received the Buddha’s exhortation and arrived in this Sahā world.
The Buddha told him:
"When you arrive in that land, pay homage, serve, and make offerings there; do not harbor indolence or pride. Bear my name and inquire after the Well-Awakened Tathāgata, saying:
'Are you dwelling in ease and comfort? Is your movement vigorous?'"

The Bodhisattvas received these instructions, prostrated at the feet of those Buddhas, and after circumambulating them seven times to the right, they suddenly vanished. They arrived in this Sahā world to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Sublime Enlightenment; they bowed their heads to his feet and each sat down to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment extended his broad and long tongue, which reached over both ears and was the color of a red utpala lotus, and declared:
"From countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, I have practiced until I attained purity; there is no falsehood in me."

The causal conditions for the sentient beings I have delivered are now complete; they are like discarded corpses left in the wilderness. Now, I shall again create conditions and establish practice anew.

Among these bodhisattvas, there are those who have established their faculties and attained power, as well as those who have first resolved their minds, and furthermore, the fourfold assembly who have not yet entered upon this path. I shall use the Buddha’s power and majestic spiritual authority to guide them, so that this great multitude may come to know the inconceivable and rare Dharma of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Many people in the world are deluded and ignorant; They do not enter the restraint of the outflows-free state, But remain within the five realms of existence, Their conduct defiled and impure."
Although I am in this Sahā world, I have rescued others from the suffering of the five desires.
Excellent! My former vow has been fulfilled today.
Just as when a person spits upon the ground, what wise person could drink it?
From incalculable eons past, I have cultivated the pure conduct of a Buddha;
casting off this body to receive another has occurred not merely for one or two eons.

If there are those of clear wisdom who, by grasping a handful of earth, can perceive the śarīra, how much more so when beholding my physical form—could there be anyone who would not attain liberation?
The cycle of birth and death is long as day and night; the ignorant remain for long in the five realms of existence.
Severing extinction, he does not abide long; seeking the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, he abides long.
Originally named Śākyamuni, he leaves behind his physical remains as śarīra for transformation;
now he shall enter the realm of emptiness, delivering sentient beings through the intermediate state.

At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these verses, eighty-four thousand nayutas of sentient beings grew weary of birth and death and all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
Furthermore, seventy billion sentient beings were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye;
seven million bodhisattvas from the realm of Māra rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, and departed with great strides.

Chapter Two: The Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment Leads the Bodhisattvas to Enter the Intermediate State to Teach and Transform At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Wondrous Enlightenment observed that the assembly was seated in perfect stillness, pure and without admixture. He perceived those who were ready to enter the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to receive the dharma of the prohibitive precepts, so as to bring great benefit and deliver immeasurable beings, establishing vast vows and performing Buddha-works.

At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment entered the Samādhi of the Invisible Crown, causing the entire great assembly and the countless billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to become of one identical color, indistinguishable from the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment himself.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa of Jambudvīpa, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas, humans and non-humans, the eight kings, and eight hundred million koṭis of sentient beings, by means of their supernormal powers, were about to enter the intermediate state (antarābhava).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses in the midst of the assembly:
“In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), beings are deluded; Confused and disoriented, they lack the Three Honored Ones.
As they turn toward the five destinies, They are led away by the force of their own past conduct.”
Some fall into the two happy realms, while others enter the three evil destinies.
How excellent!
How pitiable! Today the Tathāgata has arrived; since these beings have now attained liberation, my own vow is likewise fulfilled.
Those without form receive the teachings of form; by severing conceptualization, they sever the root of extinction.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time alike have not failed to practice this Dharma.
Material phenomena naturally blaze forth; they are extinguished through the path of concentrated mind.
The true mark of the Tathāgata is without birth and without arising or ceasing;
observing that the body is empty both internally and externally, one understands it to be a non-eternal dharma.
Conduct arises from the roots of ignorance and craving, like fire covered by ashes.
The fool thinks it has been extinguished, yet the fire remains as before.
The mind is the root of poison for humanity; good and evil follow its form.
Practice goodness and you shall go toward the good; practice evil and you shall go toward the evil.
Just as when a person commits evil deeds, They say to themselves,
"There will be no retribution later," Yet when the time for that retribution arrives, It cannot be replaced by one's kin.
One who violates the precepts and lacks the practice of the Dharma, Yet claims to be peerless in the world—
Those who go naked, eat fruits and gourds, and worship the sun, the moon, and the gods,
will fall into the three evil realms; not considering the duration of kalpas,
such as these are not sons of the Buddha, and though they may be near me, they are far from me.

At that time, after the Tathāgata Sublime Enlightenment had spoken these verses, he immediately entered the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by means of his supernatural power. There he manifested a lecture hall made of the seven treasures, a high throne of the seven treasures, and suspended silk banners and canopies; there were stairways and balustrades of gold and silver, with lapis lazuli for the ground. The bathing pools in the rear gardens were all composed of the seven treasures, where wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and various other wondrous birds warbled in harmonious chorus.

At that time, the World-Honored One again employed his supernormal powers to cause those sentient beings who were destined to die after seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, or one day, to all extend their lifespans and remain alive.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the inclinations of those sentient beings' minds and saw that they wished to be distinguished and dwell separately on one side: those of the four stages and four fruits each dwelt on one side;
those who had first resolved their minds and those in the nine abodes each dwelt on one side;
and those tending toward pratyekabuddhahood and those who had attained pratyekabuddhahood each dwelt on one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested seven hundred billion nayutas of high thrones made of the seven treasures. Upon each throne sat a manifested Buddha, and each manifested Buddha recited these four verses on impermanence:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; Consciousness takes external objects as its dharmas.
That which arises must inevitably cease; Their cessation is the supreme bliss."
Free from birth, old age, sickness, and death, Nor dwelling within the three realms of existence,
They abide forever in the realm of empty space, The sanctuary of all Buddhas.
Fearless and undefiled, unstained by sensual desire,
The fragrance of incense and the five desires are forever exhausted without remainder.
If one cuts off the hundred and eight cravings, The accumulation of phenomena is likewise extinguished.
The cessation of the former and the non-arising of the latter, as well as the realization of the fruits of the path—these are the essential summary of the Buddha-dharma:
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, wishlessness, signlessness, and emptiness; these are the path of all Buddhas.
Sentient beings of sharp faculties, upon hearing this once, do not undergo it again;
they sever [delusion] with the sword of wisdom, like fire consuming mountains and wilds.
As for classes of sentient beings who are difficult to awaken, even if a billion Buddhas stand before them, [they remain unawakened].
The roots of their transgressions are deep and firmly entrenched; though they are pitied, they are difficult to rescue.
For those receiving bodies in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and others, I shall guide them according to my verbal instructions.
Although this is not their original resolve, upon hearing the Dharma, they shall attain liberation.

At that time, while the emanated Buddha was reciting these verses, seventy-eight billion hundred thousand nayutas of beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and resolved their minds upon Bodhi.

At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment sat at the very center, ascending the seat of fearlessness. The bodhisattvas of the ten directions possessing supernatural powers sat on his left side;
Mahākāśyapa of Jambudvīpa, together with the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—sat on his right side;
and the devas, nāgas, spirits, and great kings sat behind the Buddha.

From the kings of the Four Heavenly Kings, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and so forth, they scattered flowers from mid-air as offerings and performed celestial music;
meanwhile, beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) listened to and received the Dharma teachings before the Tathāgata.
At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the sentient beings each thought to themselves:
"The Buddha is preaching the Dharma for me alone; he is not doing so for others."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s immeasurable awakening And his supernormal transformations are beyond measure.
Entering and emerging from mountains, rocks, and walls Is like a bird soaring through the void.”
Throughout incalculable eons, I have accumulated practices and piled up merit;
I deliver others without acting for my own sake, causing them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.
Nirvana has neither coming nor going, nor is there anyone seen who receives it.
Originally between the twin trees, I turned my body to come here.
When I first resolved upon the Way, I vowed to deliver all classes of sentient beings;
as long as there is even one person not delivered, I shall never abandon them.
Observe these beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), each of whom possesses superior, middling, or inferior capacities;
yet they are all defined by the threefold meaning of the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the Four Noble Truths.
Though lust, anger, and delusion may be slight, they must be eliminated through meditative concentration;
so too the eight hundred ailments of the wounds and the eighty-four thousand defilements.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom,
along with skillful means and expedient methods, uproot and sever the roots of the three poisons.
Form is originally not mine; who created this original form?
To thoroughly understand that form has no shape may be called the practice of a brahmin.
Originally, before I attained Buddhahood, I was deluded by form.
Falling into the four inverted views, they sink into the sea of birth and death.
Now, at last, one investigates the root of form and perceives that form is not real;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all these phenomena are defiled and not the true path.
The aggregates, sense bases, and eighteen elements, And the twenty-two faculties—
Each and every one is analyzed, Yet remains tranquil and free from attachment.
The intermediate state being within the desire realm,
whose defilements are all slight and thin, is like a newly made garment soiled by dust;
a person with eyes and wisdom shakes it out until all the dust is gone.
The class of beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) is likewise compared to this:
with lust, anger, and delusion attenuated, they attain awakening upon hearing the Dharma.
With a one-pointed mind that does not waver, one immediately attains the stage of Srotāpanna;
through the three turnings of the twelve factors, one further attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
by sitting and extinguishing the lower fetters, one immediately attains the path of Anāgāmin.
Suffering is exhausted and delusive craving extinguished; they have attained the state of Arhat.
Those who have entered the path of the stream are eighty billion;
those who have attained the fruit of Once-returner are eight hundred and forty billion.
Those who have attained the path of the Non-returner number one hundred twenty-two billion;
Arhats are as numerous as two *asaṃkhyeya* world-systems;
their six supernormal powers are pure and transparent throughout their bodies, and they each incline toward their respective Buddhas.
Eighty-four thousand billion;
those who aspire toward the bodhisattva mind are as numerous as motes of dust.
Their ascetic practices are beyond counting; they have given away their kingdoms, wealth, wives, and children.
Head, eyes, blood, marrow, and bones— his resolve is as firm as a diamond,
unmoved by Māra. How joyous!
"With such great merit and retribution, what wish could not be fulfilled?
At that time, the sentient beings seated there thought to themselves:
"The Buddha is preaching the Dharma for me alone, and not for the others."

Those who have entered the path of the śrāvakas and those who have attained the path of the śrāvakas; those who have entered the path of the pratyekabuddhas and those who have attained the path of the pratyekabuddhas; those who have entered the path to bodhi and those who have attained the path to bodhi.

3. Chapter on the Intermediate State within the Section on the Body: Sūtra on the Wondrous Enlightenment Tathāgata Entering the Intermediate State and Manifesting Divided Bodies, Chapter Three. At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named King of Transformed Samādhi. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

When the World-Honored One spoke these verses, there were ten billion beings in the intermediate state who harbored aspirations for the Buddha’s body—the color of purple-gold—possessing immeasurable supernormal transformations such as my own today. They vowed that in a future age they would all attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same title: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; their name was to be the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue).

Chapter Seven: Breaking the Net of Craving, from the *Bardo Sūtra*. At that time, the Tathāgata Sublime Awakening, wishing to break the fetters and proclivities of craving and cause the fourfold assembly to personally witness the evidence, immediately entered the Immovable Samādhi, desiring to make that assembly understand the craving for sense-desire, the craving for form, and the craving for the formless.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected further to himself:
"The sentient beings of this desire realm are both loved and unloved; they are both with outflows and without outflows; both conditioned and unconditioned; and both determinable and indeterminate.

The sentient beings of the form realm are neither existent nor non-existent; their consciousness is a visible dharma that is neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving. Among the three realms, desire is the heaviest; it is a defiled attachment from which one cannot separate."
Sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and others must rely upon the sacred teaching.

Among sentient beings with the five consciousnesses, there are those who come before and those who come after; among sentient beings with the consciousness of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are those who attain nirvāṇa with remainder and those who attain nirvāṇa without remainder.
How do sentient beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) encounter the Noble Ones and attain realization?

"They possess one illness: they conceive of a self as non-existent, and they constantly conceive of life as impermanent; they hold that the previous birth is not the subsequent birth, and the subsequent birth is not the previous birth."
These words of the Sage were not originally intended for those who have not yet resolved their minds;

they must be for the Sage, as in the Dharma of the Śrāvakas. "As for the consciousness of the five colors, its root is not yet established; when seeing the Buddha or cognizing the Buddha, one is attached to each instance. One may receive much merit in fortunate realms, yet those who fall are not few. Not reckoning with the self or the body, such is the practice of what is dharma and what is non-dharma. The three realms are covered by a net; though one desires to emerge, it is difficult to escape."
"Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, returns again so long as the strand remains;
so too do sentient beings of the three realms, having abandoned this [world], return once more to it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The three realms are a burning house, where the flames blaze with extreme intensity;
stained and attached by the mind of craving, one is about to enter the three evil paths.
What was produced in a prior life is not the same as what is produced in a later life; for craving possesses the nature of varying degrees of lightness and heaviness."
One who understands the Dharma of the five colors will easily cross over from this world to the next.
The eightfold path through birth and death stands at the gateway opposite Nirvana;
it is a teaching without "that" or "this," supreme and without peer.
With the supernormal power of the bases of mastery, he receives sentient beings; among those who see him, there are none who are not delivered.
Whether they be people of the future or the past, or *gandharvas*, *asuras*, devas, *nāgas*, spirits, and the like—there are none who do not attain salvation.
Excellent! Honored One of the Three Realms!
May you cause sentient beings who undergo suffering to reach the shore of the unconditioned.
Having eliminated the ailments of body, speech, and mind, one is tranquil and unmoving.
Like a hungry person obtaining food, or a thirsty person obtaining drink,
through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the fetters of craving are severed— the three gates of liberation, the nectar of immortality.

I have set forth upon the unsurpassed path; having eliminated craving and being free from thirsting thoughts, I have rescued others from the flames of suffering and attained the state of a World Hero.
To the countless Buddhas of the past, as well as those of the future and the present—
Just as I manifest transformations today, I do not conceive of "self" or "other.
The True Dharma eliminates false dharmas; Dust and defilements are forever removed.
Regarding the unimpeded dharma of *dhāraṇī*, I contemplate, discern, and observe it.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, they sport in various samādhis;
through the dharmas of the four formless concentrations, they come and go without weariness.
In the places where the Buddhas roam, there is much benefit and no diminution.
In the mere interval of lifting and setting down the foot, those delivered are beyond measure.
At every place where I set my foot, how many sentient beings are there who,
according to their respective types, attain deliverance?
Following the attainment of the three paths, there is thus no end;
The dharma of the eight liberations and non-obstruction, Transcending the faculty of life and abandoning it,
Not reckoning the perceptions of the triple world, One destroys those five heinous bonds.
When you are born, know that you are born; when you perish, know that you perish. Know your heights and know your depths;
with no place of escape in between, where can one who has transcended go?
One should know that the Buddha’s power is great; He universally enters the dharmas of *dhāraṇī*.
By virtue of his original vows, He causes those not yet crossed over to cross over.
The four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— Pervade all the ten directions.
The Buddha points out the nectar of immortality, like a compassionate mother loves her child.
Yet a mother’s love is not equal to a father’s, nor is a father’s equal to a mother’s;
the four inversions within the three realms are as difficult to transform as adamant.
Just as when an object first enters the furnace, its dust and impurities are the first to be scorched and destroyed;
that which is true does not shift, like a lotus growing from the mud.
The Buddha-way is truly authentic, fearless, and free from attachment.
“There are no burdens of conceptual thought, and the mind likewise has no coming or going.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva on the seat named Jyotiṣprabha (Inflaming Light). He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Now, as the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma of reality—whether speaking of the existence of dharmas or the non-existence of dharmas, the conditioned or the unconditioned, the determinate or the indeterminate—by what dharma do those sentient beings who receive transformation attain deliverance?”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"All dharmas are truly one; there is neither two nor three.
Whether it be craving-consciousness or non-craving-consciousness, one is forever freed from the womb."
Having severed the single bond of craving, he causes the craving of all sentient beings to be exhausted.
By the power of the Tathāgata’s divine virtue, he personally recognizes the origins of his past lives—
whether he was in the palaces of the devas or in the realms governed by a wheel-turning monarch.
"Whether in states of poverty and lowliness, or even down to the inescapable hells— discerning each and every one of these,
[I see] the defiled and attached minds of sentient beings. At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this verse,

sixty-eight billion *nayuta* of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Alas! This suffering is indeed great suffering; among all sufferings, this craving is the most painful.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to go forth."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) immediately attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Chapter Eight: The Equality of the Three Times The Intermediate State Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Equality of the Three Times At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Akṣama-kalpa (Not-Weary-of-the-Aeon). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Excellent! The supernatural power of the Tathāgata, the Most Victorious One, is most subtle and inconceivable; by means of his broad and long tongue, the Tathāgata’s divine virtue does not transgress against sentient beings.”
Regarding these three groups of sentient beings—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present—are they of the past?
Or are they of the future or the present?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Never-Weary, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

What you have asked will bring great benefit and great nourishment to sentient beings of the three categories, sever the root of ignorance, and result in the purification of bodily karma; this is not something taught by a single Buddha alone.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When a person is originally in the womb, They personally know their own past lives.
Leaving that [life] and now coming to this, The three periods of time are clearly and fixedly determined."
The former consciousness is not the present consciousness; the former body is not the present body.
Yet, due to delusion and ignorance, one does not know how to enter the gateway to the Path.
Dwelling amidst the four outflows, one gives rise to various conceptualizations.
"Alas! Old age, sickness, and death—these cause one to fall into the three periods of time.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to explain this meaning, spoke in verse:
“This self has no such form; feeling, perception, and consciousness are likewise so.
If the self is empty, those too do not exist; how then could there be consciousness, perception, or feeling?”
The formless and the named-and-formed dharmas, the conceptualizing thoughts of sentient beings—
distinguished by nine grades, they differentiate the paths of the three periods of time.
The supreme and most wondrous path is neither past nor future.
The highest of the superior is most subtle;
the upper and lower are without vitarka and vicāra.
The middle of the superior abandons the three fetters; the middle of the middling extinguishes the three stains.
Those of middle and lower capacity awaken suddenly and expansively; these are called children of the Buddha.
Though those of lower and upper capacity may seem significant, they are like bubbles upon the water—arising for a moment and then vanishing.
Among the classes of beings, those of the lower and middle grades have the deepest roots of suffering; who but I could know this?
As for the class of beings of the lowest-of-the-low, who have passed through countless kalpas, I likewise approach them to transform them, never missing an opportunity to do so.
The human mind has such variety that those on these seats do not awaken to it;
some pray for a future Buddha, while others pray for one in the present.
Such classes of sentient beings are difficult to deliver.
Human beings originally have no form when born, returning once more to empty space;
life and death are linked together—what, then, is called Nirvāṇa?
If one says there are sentient beings whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure, [how can they be liberated?]
Tranquil, they enter parinirvāṇa, free from old age and illness.
With a single mind, they give rise to great vows, yet not for their own sake.
Since empty space cannot be grasped, what can be called real or unreal?
The Tathāgata, with the Brahma-voice, distinguishes the Dharma of the true mark;
he understands the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence, the Honored One who walks alone through the three realms.
Possessing the awakened mind that perceives emptiness, he contemplates the body without attachment.
Being without perception in the third dhyāna, he advances toward the path of non-retrogression.
Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have taken this as my fundamental practice;
by means of this I became a Buddha, and it is likewise through this that I enter nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, though one accumulates merit through diligent effort, the true nature (dharmatā) is not yet attained.
Hearing that the four [noble truths] are inseparable from the four [realities], this is the seal of all Buddhas.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, immeasurable and limitless nayutas of sentient beings—including those in the intermediate state (antarābhava), those with the five-fold consciousness, and those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—sought liberation and no longer took pleasure in the three periods of time.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"What existed in the past does not exist now; the present is likewise so.
In the future, the person of Maitreya will teach and transform without distinction."
What I have now spoken is but a tiny fraction, like dust upon a fingernail;
if one were to speak of the entirety of the world-system, who could possibly exhaust it?
Though I am now dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), I shall shift my seat to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
"The person facing the gates of hell attained awakening upon hearing the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, led the beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

At that time, the World-Honored One again, by means of his supernormal power, arrived there at the sphere of consciousness of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He established and adorned high seats of the seven jewels, each of which had a manifested Buddha. Each manifested Buddha was accompanied by the fourfold assembly; every member of these assemblies was fully perfected in their dignified deportment and ritual rules. Among these sentient beings, some were reciting sutras, some were expounding the meaning, and some were the silent sages; some were entering meditative concentration, while others were emerging from it.

At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment again employed the ten powers of his supernormal faculties to receive those beings of the consciousness of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—appearing like intermediate state (antarābhava) forms, without any distinction.

At that time, the World-Honored One, according to the constant dharma and the rules of deportment of all Buddhas, caused immeasurable transformation-Buddhas to merge into a single Buddha; or he transformed a single body into immeasurable ones; or he preached the teachings of the Dharma beneath a tree; or he entered the first dhyāna with a mind undisturbed; or he was at a high cliff in a secluded and tranquil place; or while sitting in mid-air, he performed the eighteen transformations—emitting fire from his lower body and water from his upper body, emitting fire from his upper body and water from his lower body, walking upon the earth as if in space without obstruction; or he manifested parinirvāṇa, yet there was no actual passing away; or he manifested impermanence, his body bloated, putrid, and the color of a white dove; or he manifested his hands and feet each in a different location.
At that time, the beings of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, seeing this transformation, felt terror in their hearts and thought:
"In the past, we gave rise to the thought that 'concentration' was Nirvana—free from illness, free from old age, and free from all suffering and pain;
yet now we observe that this dharma is subject to birth, aging, sickness, and the pain of death."
Now that the Tathāgata has descended his spirit here, if you do not comply, the Avīci Hell shall be your dwelling.
I was originally one who made a pact with you in a previous life.
Then Piśāca Ānanda and Kalandaka saw the Buddha and prostrated themselves before him, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! Among all honored ones, you are peerless."
The descent of the Divine Spirit into this world is as rare as encountering an udumbara flower;
had the Buddha not descended his spirit here, we would have remained forever in these borderlands, slaughtering immeasurable numbers of kālaṃta birds.
He further declared:
"Now that I have encountered the Great Sage, it is like the sun dissolving the snow;
had I not encountered the Sage, I would have fallen into the body of a flying weasel, preying upon all that flies and runs, with no possibility of escape."

By virtue of this original vow, may I attain liberation from the limits of suffering; throughout the infinite realms of space, may the one of divine virtue and supreme honor in the three worlds, along with the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, all be visible to my eyes.
At that time, Kalandaka had this thought:
"We were born together in this realm of consciousness; our merits and demerits have not yet been distinguished, and we might fall into wrong views and receive the body of a flying fox."
"I originally created this body not only for the three realms—the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the five [fine-material] forms, and the formless shapes.
Once he had formed this thought, the assembly of non-percipient beings all gave rise to suffering in their minds, thinking:
"Although we have been born in this place, it is not the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, nor is it a place of peace and security."
Now that I have encountered the Tathāgata who teaches the true Dharma, I have severed and uprooted the myriad gates [of delusion], neither departing nor arriving.
Greed originally gave rise to the "self," but now I shall extinguish you.

Enshrouded by transgressions, one suffers in this life and the next; birth, old age, sickness, and pain arise like a shadow following a shadow, or as the moon and the shadows of tree leaves appear upon the water—a jackal may drink from it, yet ultimately gains nothing.
I am now the Honored One of the three periods of time; whether phenomena are real or unreal, the Dharma-transformation is unchanging. That which is born is not truly born.
Excellent! The subtle Dharma of the World is difficult to cross, yet you have crossed it.

Foolish people of the world conceive of the self as being real within the body; yet when they cast off their life-span, the bones remain linked together like hooks and chains—thus one should analyze that body.
What are life and longevity?
They are the entanglements of birth and death, suffering; having abandoned that, one undergoes this again.

There is the suffering of cold and heat while dwelling in the womb, and upon emerging, there is the sorrow of birth and extinction. Though my mother nurtured me with joy, who would not suffer if they were not born?

The body is as desolate as a water bubble; consciousness and spirit stain its form. One revolves through the five destinies, with no place of refuge wherever one goes. In the ocean of the five paths of birth and death, there is nowhere that one does not pass through.
"The mind is the root of killing the body; if you extinguish it, what cause for affliction is there for me?
Space has neither beginning nor end; who knows what is permanent and what is impermanent?
That consciousness of non-conception saw Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra—one as a king of a frontier land, the other as a winged insect.
"The three realms are the ultimate suffering; their fundamental state is not Nirvana. It is like wandering through a vast wilderness, pointing east and calling it west.
Now that we have encountered the Great Sage, we have attained liberation from all sufferings."
At that time, the beings of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception immediately spoke a verse before the Buddha, saying:
"In our former practice, we served five fires, Scorching and roasting our bodies until they were raw;
We lay upon beds of thorns, Our bodies clad in garments of skulls."
Standing on tiptoe toward the sun and moon, there was no deity they did not serve.
Now born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, they have beheld the body of the Tathāgata;
they now feel shame for their former conduct, realizing that here too there is no place of escape.
Knowing specifically the transformation of the True Dharma, the Tathāgata himself descended as a spirit;
having attained liberation from the gate of Avīci, he dwells forever in a place of peace and security.
Amidst the defilements of the five desires and birth-and-death, one is bound within the four currents.
The mind is deludedly attached to the three realms of existence; burn it with the fire of wisdom.
Those in the four destinies and the five paths of human beings do not see the beginning or end of birth;
those who are attached to consciousness and the notion of "self" are no different from me now.
At that time, the Tathāgata Sublime Awakening again replied in verse:
"You all originally thought it was real, For eighty-four thousand kalpas;
Yet the root of impermanent birth and death Is such that one dies there and returns here."
"You sentient beings have never [experienced] old age, sickness, or death;
yet you cling to one thing and seek nirvāṇa—this is not the true Dharma."
When defilements are exhausted but consciousness does not cease, one remains within the three evil realms;
if you do not realize this, it is not my fault— who else can deliver one from such hardship?
For immeasurable kalpas, I have vowed to deliver beings from birth, old age, and death.
It was not created by my former self, nor is it received by a later self.
Having originally attained the Vajra Samādhi, I now instruct and transform you:
earth cannot be made into space, and space cannot be made into earth.
Water cannot become fire, nor can fire become water.
All deluded and ignorant people claim that all things are "mine";
through their foolishness and ignorance, they mistake what is not the Way for the true and correct path.
Just as a weary person finds rest for a brief moment,
though they have traveled eighty-four thousand [yojanas], it seems to them like a single day.
For the sake of sentient beings suffering from the five types of misery, where is there that does not contain me?
Discerning the characteristics of bodily phenomena, Discerning the non-existence of empty dharmas,
The born do not see birth, Nor do they see death.
If one asks about the fundamental path of birth, It is produced by the traces of one's conduct.
Among the three evil states, the most grave is the disease of ignorance;
name-and-form and the six sense bases are the constants of this world.
Through contact, there arises the phenomenon of sensation; through sensation, there arises the craving for pleasure.
All sentient beings are deluded; Failing to recognize the twelve links of dependent origination, They are like moths throwing themselves into a flame.
The Tathāgata of Wondrous Enlightenment has said:
Because your defilements are heavy, my own mind’s defilements are likewise heavy.
Just as when I attain the Buddha-body, I pass through realms that are not yet saved;
I destroy the heaviness of mental defilements and distinguish between perception and non-perception.
The root source of the fetters is to regard the impermanent as permanent,
to speak of suffering as pleasure, to reckon the empty as existent,
and to take that which is non-self as self.
Having long practiced perversions, like moths greedy for the light of a flame,
they do not avoid the calamity of destroying their bodies.
To be born in this Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is like felling a tree.
The roots grow back again, enveloped by ignorance; now the gate of the Deathless is opened.
Within the Noble Truths and True Suchness lies the uprooting of the very foundation of suffering.
Forever extinguished without remainder.
Birth after birth, life after life, shall not be interrupted;
now I have shattered the three realms and am about to reach the further shore, the place of peace and fearlessness.

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these verses, all beings in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment, yet they did not enter parinirvāṇa within the nirvana without remainder.

To those who were destined for rebirth in the heavens, he taught the ten wholesome paths of action; to those destined for rebirth among humans, he taught the five precepts; and to those heading toward the three evil realms, he spoke of the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, the chariot of fire, and the cauldron of glowing coals.
Those of such a kind—three hundred and thirty-six billion nayutas of beings weary of the lifespan of a kalpa—hearing the pure Dharma, immediately attained the fruit of the Way.

At that time, the World-Honored One further employed his supernormal powers, the ten powers, and the fearlessnesses to receive those sentient beings of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, leading them to the realm of the five-colored consciousness-beings. He cultivated the Bodhi tree and adorned the buddha-field, emitting great radiance; from each ray of light there emerged a transformation Buddha, and each transformation Buddha sat upon a high seat of the seven treasures, possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and preached the six perfections (pāramitās).

When those sentient beings of the five colors beheld the Tathāgata’s transformation, the defilements and fetters of their minds were completely and peacefully eliminated; they no longer aspired to or took pleasure in being stained by or attached to birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse with a pure Brahma-voice:
"The root of suffering is the enmity of birth and death; It is removed through skillful means."
With the four immeasurables and great compassion, transcending the infinite realms;
now these people of sharp faculties, hearing this but once, do not undergo rebirth again;
beholding the Buddha’s physical form and marks, they universally enter the bliss of nirvana.
"Thus one knows that the path of the sages and saints is immeasurable and inconceivable;
by extinguishing defilements so they no longer arise, all become identical to the path of the sages and saints.

When the World-Honored One spoke this verse, the infinite and immeasurable beings of the five destinies were all given a single name. In a future age, they shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān named Puguang (Universally Vast).

Chapter Nine: On Non-Arising and Non-Cessation from the *Zhongyinying Wushengmie Pin Jing*. At that time, the Tathāgata Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue), being about to travel to the lands of all Buddhas, addressed the sentient beings of the three groups who had resolved their minds to seek the path to Nirvāṇa:
"I am now present here and preaching the Dharma for you; if you have any doubts, come immediately and ask me."
“Does Nirvana have arising and cessation?
At that time, the sentient beings of the three groups, having heard the words of the Tathāgata, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“From the Desire Realm up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, we have resolved our minds toward the inconceivable Dharma of the Mahāyāna; yet we have never heard of such things as conditioned or unconditioned dharmas. Which of these would remain?”
What is "without remainder"?
What is the state of a superior person?
And what is not the state of a superior person?
At that time, the World-Honored One distinguished for the beings of the three assemblies the meaning of the phrases, the meaning of the syllables, and the meaning of signlessness, saying:
"The supernatural powers of the Tathāgata consist of thirty-two dharmas."
What are these thirty-two?

They are the roots produced from the fundamental conditions of hundreds of millions of past lives; knowing the origins from which each was born—that one dies there to be born here, or dies here to be born there.
With the supernormal power of the eye, he observes all things as clearly as looking at a bead in the palm of his hand;
with the supernormal power of the ear, he hears the movements of flies and the steps of ants, as well as all subtle sounds.
Originally there were the three realms, but now the three realms do not exist.
You have received the realization of the Way, yet the minds you have awakened are each different, undergoing various transformations in the interim.
What, then, are the three realms?
"What is it that is not the three realms?
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke these words, the beings of the three groups once again gave rise to doubt.
Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those beings and wishing to grant them the contemplation of the dharma of signlessness, spoke in verse:
"What is called the head? What is called the feet?
What is called the flower?"
What is called the fruit?
A person’s life rests upon the head; once extinguished, it is like ashes, dust, or soil.
Just as the roots of a hundred grasses and trees, once pulled out, will not grow again.
Contemplate these phenomena of manifold marks: they have neither head nor feet;
whether with remainder or without remainder, know them all to be equal thereto.
If one says there is nirvāṇa, then my body and life exist in the present.
If one says there is no nirvāṇa, where would the three aggregates exist?
It is by the Buddha’s supernormal power that he causes you to know existence and non-existence.
I observe the suffering of the triple world; this both exists and does not exist.
The preceding thought is not the succeeding thought; the preceding form is not the succeeding form.

From countless kalpas ago, from the time I first lifted my foot until this very moment, within that interval I have given rise to great compassion—a state beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles.
When I gave rise to great compassion for those suffering in the three realms,
like a compassionate mother nursing her child, there was none who was not fully satisfied.
What I originally gave as a mere handful, I now obtain according to my every wish.
The various rare treasures of the seven jewels are obtained instantly according to one's thoughts;
how much more so the four immeasurables?
Who could fail to distinguish those who save sentient beings through the six perfections?
Only a Buddha knows this; I shall now explain it to you. To distinguish between that which remains and that which does not:
if one wishes to perceive my realm, I shall follow with my supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), so that upon reaching that place and attaining Buddhahood, one shall be named Śākyamuni.
In seventy-two times the sands of the Ganges, the lands to the southwest are adorned;
all are transformed by the One Way, with no pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas.
That land is exceedingly joyful; whatever one thinks of appears before one.
Unlike this world-system, which is bound by lust, anger, and delusion, a single sound pervades the four quarters; those who hear it immediately attain liberation.
In that land, the trees are made of the seven treasures;
when the wind blows upon their leaves, every leaf turns toward its neighbor, and all together proclaim the *pāramitās*.
I shall dwell within that buddha-field for an *asaṃkhyeya* of kalpas.
When I now manifest my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma I leave behind shall endure for twelve kalpas.
To know the length of these kalpas: take one day of the Bhadrakalpa as a single unit;
by calculating the number of days and nights in this manner, the twelve kalpas are completed.
"You three groups of people, do you know of my merit?
Having gone to that land in the eastern direction, eighty billion yojanas away,
that land is named Ananta (Endless), and the Buddha there is named Kṣayadhātu (Extinguished Realm)."
I appeared as a disciple in training, shaving my head and donning the kāṣāya;
kneeling for a long time, I received the noble Dharma, and that Buddha knew my mind.
Those various classes of sentient beings, seeing me wearing the dharma robes, [were inspired].
Taking no pleasure in worldly desires, they joyfully concur in leaving the household life.
Fully endowed with dignified deportment and ritual propriety, they never fail in the laws of the prohibitions and precepts;
when I bend or stretch my limbs, those who see me stand with their hair standing on end.
All these were originally bound by past karma, having made a common vow together;
they have left desire behind and are free from attachment, possessing no marks of arising or ceasing.
Having fully cultivated the holy life, through the spiritual power of me, the Buddha, [they have attained this].
Having attained liberation from death, one contemplates these states of non-discrimination and the like.
Failing to understand that birth is followed by cessation, one wanders through the five realms of existence;
yet the nectar-like Dharma of the Four Noble Truths shall satisfy all people.
When the World-Honored One spoke this verse, he saw that these novice disciples had shaved their hair and beards and received the holy teachings;
one billion seven hundred million sentient beings aspired to attain the contemplation of the Dharma through reflection, no longer delighting in the household life, and went forth to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha addressed the sentient beings of the three assemblies:
"To the northeast of here, beyond infinite and immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a buddha-field named Clear and Bright, and its Buddha is named Moonlight."
The people of that land are free from lust, anger, and ignorance, and likewise devoid of arrogance, self-conceit, and false pride.

The sentient beings of that land always delight in tranquility; sitting alone in non-action, they bind their mindfulness before them, never harboring distracted thoughts. Even amidst thunder, lightning, and thunderclaps, their minds remain unmoved.
At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue) arrived at that land and sat upon the ground; when those sentient beings saw him sitting in meditation, they all followed his example.

By means of his supernormal powers and his contemplation of the signless dharma (animitta), the Buddha turned the minds of sentient beings as easily as one turns objects with the hand, causing them to know the permanent and the impermanent, and to know the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. To some sentient beings he caused them to know mindfulness (smṛti); to some he caused them to know upholding (dhāraṇī); to some he caused them to know tranquility (praśrabdhi); and to some he caused them to know self-guarding.

When the Buddha was about to manifest the merits of the four dhyānas, he immediately, before the assembly of the three groups, entered and emerged from the first dhyāna into the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; he arose from the fourth dhyāna and entered the third, second, and first dhyānas; he proceeded from the first dhyāna to the third, and from the fourth to the second—this is called the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the Lion’s Unfurling Samādhi).

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested this supernormal power of the samādhi of mental concentration to deliver infinite and immeasurable nayutas of sentient beings, all of whom together resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Some made vows for the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; others attained the purity of the Dharma-eye or realized the path of pratyekabuddhahood.
At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment suddenly vanished from sight. Chapter Ten:

The Teaching on the Formless Emptiness of the Intermediate State. At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment cast off his intermediate state form and entered the Samādhi of the Treasury of Space; with the roar of a Buddha, he uttered eight kinds of sounds.
What are the eight? They are:
not a male voice, not a female voice, not a long voice, not a short voice, not a noble voice, not a lowly voice, not a voice of suffering, and not a voice of ambrosia.
At that time, the World-Honored One concealed his form so as not to appear, and manifested eighty-four thousand pāramitās.
What are the eighty-four thousand pāramitās?

The perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the root of the afflictions of craving and fetters; like the moon shrouded by clouds, all sentient beings are dragged by desire, subject to four hundred ailments, being born once and perishing once.
When a person has committed the five heinous crimes and wishes to escape the Avīci hell, they see the eight hells, and their hair stands on end.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, and east; because sentient beings hear these sounds, he expounds these various dharmas.
At that time, the beings of the three realms, hearing the voice from space—which was colorless and formless—perceived within it the proclamation of all dharmas:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"The teachings of all Buddhas are formless and shapeless, difficult to conceive.
At that time, the sentient beings of the three assemblies, though of diverse forms, raised their voices in unison and addressed the void in verse:
"The Tathāgata was originally here, Fully endowed with the thirty-two marks."
With compassion you pity all beings; the moisture of your grace is immeasurable.
For my sake, speak of the subtle and wondrous Eightfold Noble Path;
though your form is hidden, we hear your holy voice: that all things are impermanent.
The Tathāgata’s golden body, though originally present, is not seen now;
one hears only the sound of his voice. Since the Buddha is without self, how could there be [a self]?
Calculating the root of birth and death as a self, it wanders on without staying still.
But being deluded by form, merit perishes and sin arises.
The Tathāgata, the Great Holy Honored One, shows people how to practice all dharmas;
suddenly departing from physical forms, he comes through sound to teach and transform them.
Due to the conditions of past lives, though the form has passed away, its voice reaches me.
Old age and sickness give rise to anxiety and sorrow; four snakes bite my body:
the earth element is the bones and flesh, and the water element is the moisture.
The fire element is characterized by parching; the wind element is characterized by dispersal.
The Dharma of the Three Vehicles is free from attachment; because it is detached from existence, it exists within existence.
The defilements of the mind have long since been abandoned; yet because of the four elements, it continues to exist.
The Tathāgata, the Great Holy Honored One, has no self or other, nor the four great elements.
Right speech is of four kinds, yet it is also without four kinds;
right speech is without four kinds, yet it is also possessed of four kinds.
"This is an indeterminate dharma; who is able to bring it to ultimate completion?
At that time, the Tathāgata answered that voice and spoke in verse, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
Do you know emptiness?
All dharmas are impermanent.
Human birth is not an original birth; how could there be conditions for an original birth?
My voice and your voice—can they be apprehended or not?
For countless eons, I have never acted for the sake of even a single sentient being.
In the brief span of a single thought or a single breath, I do not grieve that few are saved.
Though those delivered are incalculable, I do not feel joy thereby.
Originally, for the sake of a single person, I remained in quietude and did not deliver others;
later, through conditions, I encountered people, yet I have not failed my original vow.
Dwelling here in Jambudvīpa, among the four castes, the Kṣatriya is supreme;
setting aside the Brāhmaṇa, all other castes are far inferior.
By means of the contemplation of the fundamental Dharma-realm, one perceives the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
I am not, and that [other] is also empty; what, then, is there of birth and death?
Those who speak of birth claim it has a source; from where does that which is born come?
If one knows the root of birth and death, Nirvana lies before me.
Understanding and knowing the dharma of nirvāṇa, there is neither Buddha nor self.
From where does the dharma arise?
To where does it go when it ceases?
The Buddha, by means of the true Dharma, manifests through the marks of existence and non-existence;
at this place of arising and ceasing, the deluded and confused attain the vision of the correct.
To say there is existence is not truly existent; to say there is non-existence is not truly non-existent.
Wandering through the ocean of birth and death, bound by the five desires;
without a driver and without a whip, one falls of one’s own accord into the abyss of saṃsāra.
Only then does one come to know sin and merit, and to understand what constitutes repentance and what does not.

At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these verses, eighty-seven billion nayutas of sentient beings from the three categories of existence realized the dharma of formlessness and resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

11. The Intermediate State Sūtra on the Realm of Form and the Formless Realm, Chapter Eleven. At that time, a bodhisattva in the assembly heard the voice of a Tathāgata in the air. Looking up into the sky, he exclaimed:
"How extraordinary!"
One hears only its sound but does not see its form;
this color is not its true color, and the other aggregates (skandhas) are likewise so.
These sentient beings of the desire realm are difficult to liberate; they must be eradicated without remainder by the sword of wisdom.
The pure conduct I originally cultivated was not created by body, speech, or mind; it was neither one nor two.

You desire that I be born from you, yet because of you I fall into the three miserable realms. If a single thought of desire is extinguished, all manifold perceptions will likewise be gone—without past, future, or present.
The Tathāgatas of the past taught and transformed all classes of sentient beings:
when they spoke of the past, they did not speak of the present or the future;
when they spoke of the future, they did not speak of the past or the present.
"He speaks of the present, but not of the past or the future;
he may say that the three periods of time exist, or he may say that the three periods of time do not exist.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to explain this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Birth, old age, sickness, and death are the root; these are the defilements of all Tathāgatas.
One must enter therein to deliver them—why then act like one who belongs to hell?”
Unlike the Honored One of Wondrous Enlightenment, who teaches within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
he is the most supreme among the supremely subtle, beyond the reach of the inferior.
Like a person holding an alms-bowl to beg, he accepts whatever is offered according to their capacity.
The bowl-bearer reflects:
"Is this existent? Is it non-existent?
To claim realization before it is realized is the root of false views.
To claim that the True Dharma is not the Dharma is to wander in the abyss of the five realms of existence.
To discern the Dharma through the True Dharma is not to lose the nature of phenomena;
if one does not lose the nature of phenomena, this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no three temporal divisions, nor does it have past, future, or present.
If you say this is the present, what exactly is that present?
If you say it is the past, what is that which is past? If you say it is the future, what is that which is future?
One who can understand this Dharma clearly comprehends the Honored One of the three periods of time.
Understanding that from the beginning there is no defiled thought, one accords with the practice of the One Great Vehicle;
for the sake of sentient beings with whom there is a karmic connection, one brings them all across without exception.
It is like a debtor who, having finished repaying their debt, desires to rejoice.
"Thoroughly penetrating both the internal and external, they move about without timidity.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Avalokiteśvara, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and his voice of instruction, spoke these verses with their divine mouths:
"The root of birth, old age, sickness, and death / Is the defilement of all Tathāgatas."
I must enter therein to deliver them; where would I not go and return?
My Master Amitāyus is never extinguished throughout eternal kalpas;
since this was my original vow, why am I now among the people of hell?
Unlike the Honored One of Wondrous Enlightenment, who teaches within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
you are supreme among the most subtle and sublime, beyond the reach of those of inferior capacity.
May I, when I later attain Buddhahood, be no different from that Wondrously Enlightened One.
At that time, when Avalokiteśvara spoke these verses, three hundred million sentient beings resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Joy from the *Zhongyin Jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State). At that time, the Tathāgata Wondrous Enlightenment entered the samādhi of quiescent extinction, intending to travel to other worlds to observe those he had delivered.

Inconceivable numbers of sentient beings felt their hearts leap with joy, like bhikṣus who have entered the dharma of the fourth dhyāna, their minds serene and tranquil, free from hunger and thirst, exclaiming: "Excellent!"
"Through this teaching, I shall not fail my original vow.
With a heart full of self-congratulation, he spoke this verse:
"The Tathāgata’s power of spiritual feet Is free from suffering, unwholesomeness, and existence."
Manifesting emanations everywhere to transform beings, he seeks to deliver those with whom he has a karmic connection.
The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and others are no different in the number they deliver;
they likewise abide within the three categories of beings, using the True Dharma to eliminate what is not the Dharma.
The Dharma-gate of ambrosia is opened, Closing off the three evil realms;
It extols great wisdom And uproots the source of ignorance.
All dharmas are naturally adorned, Pure both within and without.
The four immeasurable minds of compassion pervade everywhere without exception;
by restraining body, speech, and mind, one transcends birth, old age, and death.

At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these verses, the three groups of sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm throughout all directions received the teaching from the midst of the air; they all resolved their minds upon supreme, perfect enlightenment, joyfully accepted and practiced it, paid homage, and departed.
The Scripture on the Intermediate State, Scroll II.
